... omenirea dispune de tratate pentru păsările migratoare, pentru cafeaua care traversează frontierele și pentru astronauții care se întorc în siguranță pe Pământ, dar încă nu există un tratat echivalent pentru persoanele afectate de dezastre 🤔

❗Este o lacună extraordinară în sistemul global de protecție❗

În prezent, statele membre ale ONU lucrează la elaborarea unui nou tratat menit să contribuie la protejarea oamenilor înainte, în timpul și după dezastre naturale.

Când au loc dezastre, întârzierile costă vieți omenești. Mușcarea Internațională de Cruce Roșie și Semilună Roșie solicită reguli internaționale mai stricte, astfel încât ajutorul să poată ajunge mai repede, cooperarea să fie mai clară, iar oamenii să fie mai bine protejați.

Dacă omenirea poate conveni asupra unor reguli pentru salvarea persoanelor care se întorc din spațiu, putem conveni asupra unor reguli pentru protejarea oamenilor care trăiesc aici, pe Pământ.

FULL TEXT



       Daily Press Briefing by the Office of the Spokesperson for the Secretary-General     



         The following is a near-verbatim transcript of today's briefing by Stéphane Dujarric, Spokesman for the Secretary-General.       

         Alright, good afternoon. Thank you for your patience.       

         **Noon Briefing Guest

         In a short while, we will be joined virtually by our guest, Inger Andersen, who, as you know, is the Executive Director of the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP). She will brief on the launch of the latest UNEP report, called "Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return". The report finds that as global temperatures rise, the world must strive to return to below 1.5°C as soon as possible and simultaneously reduce the vulnerability of societies, communities and economies to climate impacts.       

         In a video message on the launch, the Secretary-General noted that humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe. He pointed out that we are set to breach the 1.5°C limit within the next few years, and this summer's scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead.       

         The Secretary-General warned that every fraction of a degree will cost lives, will destroy livelihoods, will deepen inequality and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage. He stressed that we must make the overshoot as small and short as possible, limiting how high temperatures rise and how long they remain above 1.5, and that the fight for 1.5°C is the fight for humanity.       

         So, we will get Inger very soon, and Inger, I ask for your patience.       

         **Briefings/Tomorrow

News and Press Release Nueva York/Ginebra, 3 de septiembre de 2026 – La Federación Internacional de Sociedades de la Cruz Roja y de la Media

Luna Roja (IFRC) lanza hoy su nueva campaña mundial, "El tratado que le falta a la Tierra", para mostrar una cruda realidad: mientras que el derecho internacional protege a astronautas en situaciones de peligro, no existe ningún tratado internacional integral que establezca cómo deben cooperar los países para proteger a las personas en casos de desastre.

Un tratado global proporcionaría un marco común para la cooperación internacional antes de que se produzcan los desastres, y en caso de que se necesite ayuda internacional. En la práctica, esto podría traducirse en un despliegue más rápido de los equipos humanitarios, trámites aduaneros y fronterizos más sencillos para los suministros de primera necesidad, una cooperación más predecible entre los gobiernos y las organizaciones humanitarias, menores costos y menos trabas administrativas, así como una mejor protección para las personas afectadas por los desastres.

De forma paralela al lanzamiento de la campaña, la IFRC publica un nuevo análisis global que muestra por qué es necesario un tratado sobre desastres y qué diferencia podría suponer. El estudio recopila datos sobre el riesgo de desastres, la protección y los obstáculos a la ayuda internacional, junto con cuatro estudios de caso de Belice, Fiyi, Líbano y Madagascar.

Lea los estudios de caso de Belice, Fiyi, Líbano y Madagascar.

En 2027, los gobiernos se reunirán para negociar el tratado, y la IFRC pone a su disposición su apoyo a lo largo de todo el proceso, ofreciendo conocimientos técnicos y décadas de experiencia en la preparación y respuesta ante desastres.

La campaña de la IFRC cuenta con el respaldo de destacados astronautas, entre los que se encuentran la Dra. Sian Proctor, Nicole Stott, José Hernández, Scott Kelly, Doug Hurley, Julie Payette, Jean-François Clervoy y Do

É por isso que a 𝐂𝐫𝐮𝐳 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐥𝐡𝐚 𝐝𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐛𝐨 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐞 𝐚𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐚 𝐨 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐨 𝐪𝐮𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐚 𝐚̀ 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐚.

𝐎𝐬 𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐚𝐬 𝐬𝐚̃𝐨 𝐩𝐫𝐨𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐢𝐝𝐨𝐬 𝐩𝐨𝐫 𝐮𝐦 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐨.
𝐀𝐬 𝐩𝐞𝐬𝐬𝐨𝐚𝐬 𝐞𝐦 𝐜𝐚𝐭𝐚́𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐞 𝐭𝐚𝐦𝐛𝐞́𝐦 𝐝𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐚𝐦 𝐬𝐞𝐫.

Quando a catástrofe acontece, os atrasos custam vidas. A 𝐅𝐞𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐜̧𝐚̃𝐨 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫𝐧𝐚𝐜𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐚 𝐂𝐫𝐮𝐳 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐥𝐡𝐚 𝐞 𝐝𝐨 𝐂𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐦𝐞𝐥𝐡𝐨 apela a regras internacionais mais fortes, para que a ajuda chegue mais depressa, a cooperação seja mais clara e as pessoas fiquem mais protegidas.

Os Estados membros da ONU estão a trabalhar num novo tratado para ajudar a proteger as pessoas antes, durante e depois das catástrofes.

𝐀𝐩𝐨𝐢𝐞 𝐨 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐚𝐝𝐨 𝐪𝐮𝐞 𝐅𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐚 𝐚̀ 𝐓𝐞𝐫𝐫𝐚. 𝐏𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐢𝐥𝐡𝐞 𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐚 𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐬𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐦.

La Fédération internationale des sociétés nationales de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (FICR) lance une campagne mondiale pour un traité mondial contre les désastres. Dévoilée jeudi, celle-ci s'appuie sur le soutien de six astronautes.

L'astronaute français Jean-Francois Clervoy (à droite) soutient l'action de la FICR (archives). Keystone/AP/STR

© KEYSTONE

Les Etats se réuniront en 2027 pour négocier un traité international sur les catastrophes. La FICR, étable à Genève, les accompagne avec son expérience technique et des décennies de préparation aux désastres.

"Le droit international protège les astronautes", mais "il n'y a pas de traité international sur la manière avec laquelle les pays devraient collaborer pour protéger des personnes avant, pendant et après un désastre", déplore la FICR.

Cet accord pourrait notamment un déploiement plus rapide des travailleurs humanitaires, des procédures douanières facilitées pour le matériel et une collaboration plus prévisible entre gouvernements et organisations humanitaires. Les coûts seraient plus bas et les barrières administratives seraient moins importantes, selon l'institution.

De quoi mieux protéger les personnes affectées. "Chaque heure perdue en raison de barrières légales ou administratives" peut empêcher de sauver des victimes, affirme le secrétaire général de la FICR Jagan Chapagain.

En 2025, 358 désastres naturels ont eu des effets pour plus de 110 millions d'individus. Les pertes économiques ont atteint plus de 169 milliards de dollars. Certains matériels humanitaires sont taxés deux fois que les autres marchandises.

Dans de nombreux pays exposés aux désastres, les procédures douanières prennent habituellement environ 11 jours. Et environ 60% des approvisionnements qui arrivent portent sur des biens qui ne sont pas urgents et n'auraient pas dû être envoyés, rendant plus difficile le travail des humanitaires en termes de personnel, de stockage et de distr

items.text:
La Fédération internationale des Sociétés de la Croix-Rouge et du Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) a lancé jeudi une campagne mondiale, baptisée « Earth's Missing Treaty », pour appeler les États à adopter le premier traité international global consacré à la protection des personnes avant, pendant et après les catastrophes, alors que le droit international prévoit déjà des mécanismes de protection pour les astronautes en détresse.

Les États membres de l'ONU ont accepté d'engager des négociations sur un « Traité sur la protection des personnes en cas de catastrophe », qui doivent débuter en 2027, et l'IFRC entend apporter son expertise au processus.

Selon la Fédération, un tel instrument créerait un cadre commun pour faciliter la coopération internationale avant les catastrophes et accélérer l'acheminement de l'aide lorsque celles-ci surviennent, notamment grâce à des procédures douanières et frontalières simplifiées, une coopération plus prévisible entre gouvernements et organisations humanitaires, une réduction des coûts et des obstacles administratifs et une meilleure protection des populations sinistrées.

L'IFRC appuie sa campagne sur une nouvelle analyse mondiale, fondée notamment sur des données relatives aux risques de catastrophe, à la protection et aux entraves à l'aide internationale, ainsi que sur des études de cas consacrées au Belize, aux Fidji, au Liban et à Madagascar.

Elle souligne qu'en 2025, 358 catastrophes liées à des aléas naturels ont touché plus de 110,2 millions de personnes dans le monde et provoqué quelque 169,7 milliards de dollars de pertes économiques, selon la base EM-DAT (Emergency Events Database).

Les obstacles administratifs peuvent également retarder l'arrivée de personnels humanitaires, d'équipements spécialisés et de produits de première nécessité: en l'absence d'exemptions, les couvertures, tentes et autres articles essentiels peuvent être soumis à des droits de douane moyens d'environ 17% dans le monde,

03/09/2026 | Press release International treaties protect astronauts in distress. But if a flood strikes your city, there is still no comprehensive

global treaty to help countries cut through red tape and coordinate international assistance.

New York/Geneva, 3 September 2026 – The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is today launching a new global campaign, Earth’s Missing Treaty, to highlight a stark reality: while international law protects astronauts in distress, there is no comprehensive international treaty setting out how countries should cooperate to protect people before, during and after disasters.

The campaign highlights IFRC’s call for countries to support the adoption of the Treaty on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters, which UN Member States have agreed to negotiate and which would be the first comprehensive global treaty dedicated to protecting people before, during and after disasters.

A global treaty would provide a common framework for international cooperation before disasters strike and when international assistance is needed. In practice, this could mean faster deployment of humanitarian teams, simpler customs and border procedures for life-saving supplies, more predictable cooperation between governments and humanitarian organisations, lower costs and fewer administrative barriers, and better protection for people affected by disasters.

Alongside the campaign, IFRC is publishing new global analysis showing why a disaster treaty is needed and the difference it could make. The research brings together data on disaster risk, protection and barriers to international assistance, alongside four country case studies from Belize, Fiji, Lebanon and Madagascar.

Image by magnific When a cyclone destroyed Chompa Munda's home in coastal Bangladesh in 2019, she and her son went days without food.

When the next one came in 2024, her phone lit up hours before it made landfall.

A US$43 transfer was sent straight to her bank account because a weather forecast had crossed an agreed threshold. She bought food, drinking water and candles, and left for a storm shelter.

Cyclone Remal still flooded her house, but the money had already arrived. The leftover funds helped her rebuild. Funding was released a day before the storm hit, meaning 150,000 people had cash in hand. No appeal, no assessment, no waiting for anyone to decide.

The same idea is now being tried with entire national budgets

Jamaica has been through the same two-storm sequence . Hurricane Beryl struck in July 2024, causing damage worth 1.9% of GDP. It was the third most destructive storm to hit the island in 25 years. The country had prepared, with a catastrophe bond, insurance and loans. The insurance paid out to the tune of US$26.9m . The bond paid nothing at all. Had Beryl run 15km further north, it would have released US$45m in bonds, but the storm passed just south and the threshold went unmet.

Sixteen months later came Hurricane Melissa, the strongest ever recorded to hit Jamaica, hitting more than 40% of GDP. Within days, the government mobilised US$662m in liquidity from national reserve funds, Caribbean parametric insurance, a catastrophe bond plus contingent facilities from the World Bank and the Inter-American Development Bank, arranged long beforehand. The difference between Beryl and Melissa was disaster risk finance working in a system at scale. Melissa was severe enough to trigger all of it at once.

News and Press Release International treaties protect astronauts in distress.

But if a flood strikes your city, there is still no comprehensive global treaty to help countries cut through red tape and coordinate international assistance.

New York/Geneva, 3 September 2026 – The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies (IFRC) is today launching a new global campaign, Earth's Missing Treaty , to highlight a stark reality: while international law protects astronauts in distress, there is no comprehensive international treaty setting out how countries should cooperate to protect people before, during and after disasters.

The campaign highlights IFRC's call for countries to support the adoption of the Treaty on the Protection of Persons in the Event of Disasters, which UN Member States have agreed to negotiate and which would be the first comprehensive global treaty dedicated to protecting people before, during and after disasters.

A global treaty would provide a common framework for international cooperation before disasters strike and when international assistance is needed. In practice, this could mean faster deployment of humanitarian teams, simpler customs and border procedures for life-saving supplies, more predictable cooperation between governments and humanitarian organisations, lower costs and fewer administrative barriers, and better protection for people affected by disasters.

Alongside the campaign, IFRC is publishing new global analysis showing why a disaster treaty is needed and the difference it could make. The research brings together data on disaster risk, protection and barriers to international assistance, alongside four country case studies from Belize, Fiji, Lebanon and Madagascar.

Croissant-Rouge (IFRC) lance aujourd'hui une nouvelle campagne mondiale, intitulée Earth's Missing Treaty (Le traité manquant de la Terre), afin de mettre en lumière une réalité frappante : alors que le droit international impose une obligation globale de secourir les astronautes en détresse, il n'existe aucun traité international global définissant la manière dont les pays doivent coopérer pour protéger les populations avant, pendant et après une catastrophe.

Cette campagne vient soutenir l'appel de l'IFRC pour que les États s'engagent en faveur de l'adoption du Traité sur la protection des personnes en cas de catastrophe. Actuellement négocié par les États membres de l'ONU, ce texte constitue le tout premier traité mondial d'envergure dédié à la protection des populations face aux crises humanitaires majeures.

Un traité mondial offrirait un cadre commun pour la coopération internationale, aussi bien en amont des catastrophes qu'au moment où l'aide internationale devient nécessaire. En pratique, cela se traduirait par un déploiement plus rapide des équipes humanitaires, des procédures douanières et frontalières simplifiées pour l'acheminement des secours vitaux, une coopération plus prévisible entre les gouvernements et les organisations humanitaires, une réduction des coûts et des barrières administratives, ainsi qu'une meilleure protection des populations touchées par les catastrophes.

Cette année, l'IFRC a publié quatre études de cas analysant l'impact potentiel de ce traité sur la protection des personnes lors de catastrophes au Belize, aux Fidji, au Liban et à Madagascar.

Photo caption: Nellie Evison – 2026 UC Master of Laws graduate.

A comparative study by Te Whare Wānanga o Waitaha | University of Canterbury (UC) Master of Laws graduate Nellie Evison found that legal protections and emergency response provisions for utility workers after disasters in New Zealand and the United States were often voluntary or not explicit.

“Utility workers are essential to restoring power, water and other critical services after a disaster, and they can face many of the same hazards as emergency responders. Having clear legal protections helps to keep them safe, clarifies responsibilities and supports a faster, more coordinated recovery,” Evison says.

Working with QuakeCoRE, a Centre of Research Excellence that aims to improve earthquake resilience, along with the specialist knowledge Evison developed through her research, have helped launch her career. Before graduating, she secured a Wellington-based role at the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE) as an advisor in incident management and emergency management.

Evison believes her familiarity with New Zealand's Coordinated Incident Management System was a key factor in gaining her role at MBIE.

“I looked at it a lot during my master's, so the theoretical knowledge I acquired through my research has been directly applicable to what I am doing,” she says.

Her team helps build emergency management and business continuity capability across MBIE and supports incident management teams during local and national responses. Evison has already put her knowledge into practice in the logistics function during responses.

While she is not working as a lawyer or providing legal advice, Evison says her UC Law education prepared her for a career extending well beyond conventional legal practice. “The writing, research and critical thinking skills you learn throughout an undergraduate degree and master's are applicable to so many different jobs,” s

Noon briefing of 2 September 2026 CLIMATE REPORT/OVERSHOOT

In a video message on the launch of the latest UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report, called “Limiting Overshoot: Navigating exceedance of 1.5°C and pathways towards return”, the Secretary-General noted that humanity is speeding past the limit to avoid climate catastrophe. He pointed out that we are set to breach the 1.5 degree limit within the next few years, and this summer's scorching heat, raging wildfires and deadly floods are a warning of what lies ahead.

The Secretary-General warned that every fraction of a degree will cost lives, will destroy livelihoods, will deepen

inequality and push ecosystems closer to irreversible damage. He stressed that we must make the overshoot as small and short as possible, limiting how high temperatures rise and how long they remain above 1.5, and that the fight for 1.5 degrees is the fight for humanity.

IRAN

The Secretary-General is gravely concerned by the renewed exchanges of fire overnight between the United States and the Islamic Republic of Iran. The Secretary-General is deeply alarmed by reports of civilian casualties, including in a strike that reportedly hit a wedding ceremony in Iran. The Secretary-General condemns all attacks against civilians. He recalls that all parties must respect their obligations under international humanitarian law, including the principles of distinction, proportionality, and precaution.

As we have seen, few countries in the region are immune from this escalation, with airspace and critical shipping routes continuing to be heavily impacted.

The Secretary-General reiterates his call for an immediate cessation of military action and urges all concerned to exercise restraint and refrain from actions and rhetoric that could further escalate already high tensions.

Further escalation, as you can imagine, would have devastating consequences for civilians and for the wider region
